description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
Output 1 - 16 staff members of MSU (at least 50% women) have the capacity to develop, implement and evaluation effective trainings for adults on inclusive governance, decentralisation and the role of local governments in sustaining peace.
Output 2 - 16 staff members of MSU (at least 50% women) have increased awareness on the importance of transparency, accountability and citizen participation, gender and conflict sensitivity.
Output 1 and 2 were accomplished through the following activities:
- Online ToT on adult training methods (12 April – 2 May 2021): 18 participants successfully completed the training (9 male, 9 female) - Online ToT on inclusive governance (26 October – 21 November 2021): 18 participants successfully completed the training (9 male, 9 female) - Face-to-face ToT on sustaining peace, the role of local governments and action planning (16-19 May 2022, Cagayan de Oro): 14 participants successfully completed the training (7 male, 7 female). Unfortunately, not all selected trainers could attend as some of them had other professional responsibilities that week.
The evaluation of programme, see above data on the indicators, showed that the trainees met the objectives and realised the outputs.
Output 3 - 16 staff members of MSU (at least 50% women) have developed and use personal development plans.
At the end of the online ToT on adult training methods (12 April – 2 May 2021): the participants developed a personal action plan to implement the gained knowledge and skills in their professional activities. At the beginning of each of the follow-up trainings, we invited the trainees to share their experiences and lessons learned with the group, as such creating a stimulating learning environment between the participants.
Output 4 - CPA and ILG and other relevant colleges have developed SMART action plans on how to integrate the gained knowledge and skills in the organisations.
Action planning was an integrated part of the TMT strategy and training programme. At the end of the face-to-face ToT on sustaining peace, the role of local governments and action planning (16-19 May 2022, Cagayan de Oro) 3 action plans were developed and validated: one on integrating the TMT materials in the MSU curriculum, one on organising trainings for BARMM LGUs by MSU staff and one on institutional collaboration between MSU and BARMM.

comment.narrative: 07-12-2022: Organisations strengthened: MSU (its College of Public Affairs (CPA), its Institute of Local Governance (ILG) and different faculties), Cotabato City Polytechnic College, Bangsamoro Development Agency, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) It can be safely said that all included MSU campuses have been considerably strengthened as a direct result of the TMT programme. They are now undertaking training programmes and conducting in class exercises that are drawn directly from the trainings received from THA. Reportedly, workshops are happening now in various places in the Bangsamoro wherein capacity strengthening of community staff as well as other faculty members is taking place. More such transfer of knowledge and skills will continue over the coming weeks and months. At the end of the last ToT, we asked the TMT participants to reflect and discuss on this indicator through a Mentimeter questionnaire. The participants could rate the topics on a scale from 0 to 5. We present the average score for each of the questions: • To what extent do you think the training materials and methods can assist MSU to deliver effective trainings for LGUs (Local Government Unit) and their CSOs?: 4.9 • To what extent do you think the training materials and methods can assist LGUs in BARMM to establish more inclusive policies and services?: 4.6 • To what extent do you think the training materials and methods can assist LGUs in BARMM to sustain peace in their communities?: 4.3

comment.narrative: 07-12-2022: The measures presented below aimed to facilitate a safe and stimulating learning environment for all participants, both man and women. 1. We selected the participants in a gender-sensitive manner by promoting equal participation of women and men. 2. We assured that all course descriptions and learning objectives supported gender‐sensitive perspectives, attitudes, and competencies. 3. All trainers and experts were trained on and experienced in gender issues. 4. At the start of each training, a ‘code of conduct’ or ‘ground rules for working together’ was established by the participants including instruments to deal with non-gender sensitive behaviour. 5. During the online and face-to-face trainings, we encouraged all participants' active participation through various training methods, considering gender dynamics, power dynamics, culture, and being conflict sensitive. In the Bangsamoro context, it is crucial to be aware of the participants' background (cultural) and how this may affect women/men power relations and roles during the training. 6. Forums for written discussions were made available on the online platform of the training course. This gave the opportunity to all participants who did not feel comfortable speaking during the live sessions to still express themselves and receive feedback from the experts and training team. 7. For the face-to-face training in Cagayan de Oro (16-19 May 2022), one of the selection criteria for the accommodation was having enough rooms so female participants would not have to share a room with their male colleagues. The hotel was spacious and had different sitting areas which allowed female participants to have access to a women-only public space if they preferred/needed. These measures ensured that the females in the group felt safe and comfortable. 8.
